questions.title: What happens after death?
questions.asked: What do Christians, Muslims and Jews believe happens when you die?
questions.short: All three teach that the soul survives death and that God will raise the dead and judge them. They differ on what happens in between, on who is saved, and Judaism says far less about it than the other two.

body: All three faiths teach a final resurrection of the body and a judgment by God, and all three believe the person continues to exist in some way between death and that day. What fills the gap, and how much detail is given, differs a great deal.
**Christianity:** the soul goes at once into God's presence or away from it, then is reunited with a raised body at Christ's return.
**Islam:** the soul waits in the barzakh, a barrier between death and resurrection, is questioned in the grave, then is raised and judged.
**Judaism:** the Hebrew Bible says little; rabbinic Judaism teaches the World to Come and the resurrection of the dead, with much left undefined.

Jesus tells the dying thief “today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43), and Paul says he would rather “depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23, 2 Corinthians 5:8). Death is followed by judgment (Hebrews 9:27), and at the end all the dead will rise, “those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29, Revelation 20:12–15).

The Catholic Church teaches that those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified pass through purgatory before heaven, and that the living can help them by prayer and the Mass. It points to the prayer for the dead in 2 Maccabees 12:44–46 (a book Protestants do not accept as scripture) and to the man “saved, but as through fire” in 1 Corinthians 3:15.
The Orthodox pray for the dead and speak of an intermediate state in which the soul has a foretaste of heaven or hell, but reject the Latin doctrine of purgatory as a place of satisfying punishment.

Protestants reject purgatory and prayers for the dead: believers go straight to be with Christ. A minority (Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses and some others) teach “soul sleep”, that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, citing Ecclesiastes 9:5.

“Every soul will taste of death” (Quran 3:185). When death comes, the dying person begs to be sent back, but “behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised” (Quran 23:99–100). Hadith describe two angels who sit the dead person up in the grave and ask about Muhammad; the believer is shown his place in Paradise, the unbeliever fails the test (Sahih al-Bukhari 1338).

On the Day of Resurrection every deed is weighed: “whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, and whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then” (Quran 99:7–8). Sunni and Shia Muslims share this framework.

The older books of the Hebrew Bible picture the dead in Sheol, a shadowy place with no praise of God (Psalm 6:5), and say the spirit “returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The clearest resurrection text is late: Daniel 12:2.

The Mishnah makes resurrection a core belief: “all Israel have a share in the World to Come”, except, among others, one who denies that resurrection is taught in the Torah (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). It calls this world “a vestibule before the world to come” (Mishnah Avot 4:16). Reform Judaism historically replaced bodily resurrection with the immortality of the soul.

Historians note that belief in individual resurrection appears only late in Israel's history, around the second century BC, and was still disputed in Jesus' day: the Sadducees rejected it. Christianity and Islam inherited the developed form, then added far more detail.

questions.title: Is there a hell, and is it forever?
questions.asked: Do Jews believe in hell? Is hell eternal in Christianity and Islam?
questions.short: Christianity and Islam both teach a hell of fire after the judgment, and mainstream teaching in both says it is eternal for unbelievers. Judaism has Gehinnom, but most rabbinic sources make it a temporary purging of at most twelve months for all but the worst.

body: Yes in all three, but they mean different things. For most Christians and Muslims hell is eternal punishment for those who reject God. In rabbinic Judaism, Gehinnom is mostly a place of temporary purification, and Jews talk about it far less.

Jesus speaks of hell more than anyone else in the New Testament: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46), and of Gehenna “where their worm doesn't die, and the fire is not quenched” (Mark 9:43–48, quoting Isaiah 66:24). The parable of the rich man shows conscious torment in Hades (Luke 16:23–24), and Revelation ends with the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14–15).

Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches teach that hell is eternal. Two minority views have grown: annihilationism (the lost are destroyed, not tormented for ever), held by some evangelicals and Adventists, and universalism (all are eventually saved), condemned by the councils but defended by some modern theologians.

The Quran describes Jahannam often and graphically: “as often as their skins are consumed We shall exchange them for fresh skins” (Quran 4:56). Unbelievers abide in it “so long as the heavens and the earth endure save for that which thy Lord willeth” (Quran 11:106–107).

Sunni and Shia doctrine both hold that believing Muslims who sinned may be punished for a time and then brought out: hadith say God will order out of hell everyone with faith “equal to the weight of a grain of mustard seed” (Sahih al-Bukhari 22). Hell is eternal for unbelievers in mainstream teaching, though a few classical scholars, including Ibn Taymiyya by some accounts, discussed whether the Fire itself would end.

The Hebrew Bible has no developed hell. The rabbis took the name Gehinnom from a valley outside Jerusalem. The Mishnah says: “the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months” (Mishnah Eduyot 2:10). The Talmud adds that the worst offenders, such as heretics and those who deny the resurrection, descend there and are punished for all generations (Rosh Hashanah 17a).
Many modern Jews do not believe in any literal hell, and the subject plays little part in Jewish preaching.

The strongest objection is moral: eternal torment for finite wrongs, often for wrong belief rather than wrong action, seems out of proportion to critics in every tradition. Defenders reply that hell is the soul's own choice to be without God, and that God's justice cannot be measured by human standards.

questions.title: What is heaven or paradise like?
questions.asked: How do the Bible and the Quran describe heaven? Are there 72 virgins?
questions.short: The New Testament describes heaven mainly as God's presence, without marriage. The Quran describes a garden of physical pleasures, including wives with wide eyes. The number 72 is not in the Quran; it comes from a hadith.

body: The New Testament says little about the physical life of heaven and stresses seeing God. The Quran gives detailed images of gardens, rivers, food, wine that does not intoxicate and companions. The Talmud describes the World to Come as a place with no eating or drinking at all.

Revelation's picture is a city: “he will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more” (Revelation 21:4), with gates of pearl, streets of gold and no temple, “for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (Revelation 21:21–23). Jesus says that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), and Paul says it is beyond imagination (1 Corinthians 2:9).
Catholic and Orthodox teaching centres on the beatific vision, seeing God face to face. Many Protestants emphasise the renewed earth of Revelation 21.

The Quran's Paradise (al-Janna) has “rivers of water unpolluted, and rivers of milk… and rivers of wine delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of clear-run honey” (Quran 47:15). The wine gives “no aching of the head nor any madness” (Quran 56:19). The righteous are wed to companions “with wide, lovely eyes” (Quran 44:54, Quran 56:22–24), “whom neither man nor jinni will have touched before them” (Quran 55:56). It is promised to believing men and women alike (Quran 9:72).

The number seventy-two comes from a hadith about the martyr, who “is married to seventy two wives along Al-Huril-'Ayn of Paradise” (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1663, graded hasan sahih by Tirmidhi). Another hadith says God has prepared “things which have never been seen by an eye, or heard by an ear” (Sahih al-Bukhari 3244), the same idea as 1 Corinthians 2:9.
Many Muslim scholars stress that the greatest reward is seeing God, and some read the physical descriptions as real but beyond our understanding.

The Talmud quotes Rav: “In the World-to-Come there is no eating, no drinking, no procreation… Rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads, enjoying the splendor of the Divine Presence” (Berakhot 17a). Jewish tradition leaves most details undefined.

Christian and secular critics have long mocked the Quran's sensual Paradise, especially the houris, as a male fantasy. Muslims reply that the Bible also uses physical images (a banquet, a city of gold), that the women of Paradise are promised rewards too, and that the Quran's language is meant to move a desert audience. A fringe academic theory (Christoph Luxenberg) reads the word for houris as “white grapes”; most scholars of Arabic reject it.

questions.title: Is pork forbidden, and why?
questions.asked: Why can't Jews and Muslims eat pork? Can Christians? What is kosher and halal?
questions.short: The Torah forbids pork and the Quran forbids it again. Most Christians eat it because the New Testament declares foods clean. None of the texts gives health as the reason.

body: Pork is forbidden in Judaism and Islam and allowed in almost all of Christianity. The Torah's reason is that the pig divides the hoof but does not chew the cud, so it fails the test for clean animals. The Quran calls it impure. Neither text mentions disease.

Kosher law covers far more than pork. Land animals must both chew the cud and have split hooves (Leviticus 11:3, Deuteronomy 14:8); fish need fins and scales, so shellfish are banned; meat must be slaughtered by a trained shochet and drained of blood; and the command “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk” (Exodus 23:19) became the rule against mixing meat and dairy.

The rabbis classed these laws as chukim, decrees whose reasons are not given, kept because God commanded them. Maimonides suggested health reasons, but most Jewish teachers treat kashrut as a discipline of holiness.

The Quran forbids four things repeatedly: carrion, blood, pork and meat dedicated to other than God (Quran 2:173, Quran 5:3, Quran 6:145). It allows anything in real necessity, “without craving or transgression”. The rest of the list is short compared with Jewish law: shellfish are allowed by most schools.

“The food of those who have received the Scripture is lawful for you” (Quran 5:5), which many scholars apply to kosher meat and some to meat slaughtered by Christians. Shia jurists are generally stricter and require a Muslim slaughterer.

Mark says that Jesus, teaching that what goes into the mouth does not defile, was “making all foods clean” (Mark 7:18–19). Older translations such as the King James render the phrase differently, but the main point, that food does not defile, is in every version. Peter's vision tells him “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean” (Acts 10:13–15), and Paul says nothing is unclean of itself (Romans 14:14).
The apostles still asked non-Jewish converts to avoid blood and strangled meat (Acts 15:29). The Ethiopian Orthodox Church and Seventh-day Adventists keep the Old Testament ban on pork.

The popular claim that the pork ban was ancient food safety (trichinosis) is not in any of the texts and does not explain why camels and rabbits are also banned. Anthropologists such as Mary Douglas argued the laws sort animals into categories that mark Israel off from its neighbours. Archaeologists find pig bones largely absent from early Israelite sites, suggesting the avoidance is very old.

questions.title: Is alcohol forbidden?
questions.asked: Why is alcohol haram in Islam but Jesus turned water into wine?
questions.short: Islam forbids all intoxicants. Judaism and Christianity allow wine and use it in worship but condemn drunkenness. Some Protestant churches ask members to abstain completely.

body: Islam is the only one of the three that forbids drinking outright. The Bible praises wine as God's gift (Psalm 104:15) and warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 20:1). Jews bless God over wine every Sabbath; most Christians drink it at communion.

The Quran's rulings come in stages. First: in wine and gambling “is great sin, and (some) utility for men; but the sin of them is greater” (Quran 2:219). Then: do not come to prayer drunk (Quran 4:43). Finally: wine and gambling are “an infamy of Satan's handiwork. Leave it aside” (Quran 5:90–91).

Muhammad extended the ban beyond grape wine: “Every intoxicant is Khamr and every intoxicant is forbidden” (Sahih Muslim 2003). Sunni and Shia law agree. The Hanafi school once allowed small amounts of some non-grape drinks short of intoxication, but this view has largely been abandoned. Paradise has rivers of wine that do not intoxicate (Quran 47:15).

Wine is central to Jewish ritual: kiddush on Sabbath and festivals, four cups at the Passover seder, the wedding blessings. Noah's drunkenness (Genesis 9:20–21) is a warning, and the Nazirite vows abstinence (Numbers 6:3). The Talmud even says a person should drink on Purim “until he does not know how to distinguish between cursed is Haman and blessed is Mordecai” (Megillah 7b), though many later authorities limited this.

Jesus' first sign in John's Gospel is turning water into a large quantity of good wine at a wedding (John 2:9–10). Paul tells Timothy to “use a little wine for your stomach's sake” (1 Timothy 5:23) and tells all believers “Don't be drunken with wine” (Ephesians 5:18).

Catholic and Orthodox churches use wine in the Eucharist. In the 19th century many Methodists, Baptists and others adopted total abstinence and replaced communion wine with grape juice; some still require it. Their argument is prudence, not a biblical ban.

Critics point out that the Quran first describes some benefit in wine and later bans it, which Muslims explain as gradual legislation and critics as a ruling that changed with circumstances in Medina. Christians who abstain are sometimes accused of reading their own culture into a Bible that clearly approves of wine.

questions.title: Why do Muslims pray five times a day, and how do Jews and Christians pray?
questions.asked: Why five prayers? Where is that in the Quran? How often do Jews and Christians pray?
questions.short: Muslims pray five set prayers because of hadith; the Quran names prayer times but never says “five”. Jews pray three set services a day. Christians have no single binding rule, though older churches keep fixed hours.

body: All three faiths have set daily prayer. Islam has five (salat), Judaism three, and Christianity a pattern of fixed hours in its older churches and freer prayer among most Protestants. All three inherited the habit from Israel: Daniel prayed three times a day facing Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10), and a psalm says “Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out” (Psalm 55:17).

The Quran commands prayer “at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night” (Quran 11:114), from the sun's decline to the dark of night and at dawn (Quran 17:78), and says prayer is prescribed at set times (Quran 4:103). It never lists five prayers by name or number.

The number comes from hadith. In the account of the Night Journey, God first ordered fifty prayers; on Moses' advice Muhammad asked for less until God said “These are five prayers and they are all (equal to) fifty” (Sahih al-Bukhari 349). Muhammad compared them to bathing in a river five times a day (Sahih al-Bukhari 528).
Sunnis normally pray five times at five separate times, combining prayers only when travelling or in hardship.

Shia Muslims also pray five prayers but usually combine them into three sessions (noon with afternoon, sunset with night). They cite a hadith in Sunni books: Ibn Abbas reported that Muhammad prayed noon and afternoon together, and sunset and night together, “without being in a state of fear or in a state of journey” (Sahih Muslim 705).

Jews pray Shacharit (morning), Mincha (afternoon) and Maariv (evening). The Talmud records two opinions about their origin: that the patriarchs instituted them, Abraham the morning, Isaac the afternoon and Jacob the evening, or that they replace the daily Temple offerings (Berakhot 26b). The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–9) is said morning and night. Communal prayer needs a minyan of ten; Orthodox Judaism counts only men.

Jesus taught the Lord's Prayer and warned against praying for show (Matthew 6:5–13). Paul says “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). The apostles still went to the Temple “at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour” (Acts 3:1). The early Christian manual called the Didache tells believers to say the Lord's Prayer three times a day.
Catholic and Orthodox clergy and monks pray the Liturgy of the Hours at fixed times through the day. Most Protestants have no required hours and value spontaneous prayer.

Quranists, a small Muslim movement that rejects hadith, argue from the Quran alone for two or three daily prayers. Mainstream Sunni and Shia scholars answer that the Quran itself tells Muslims to obey the Prophet and that the five prayers were practised continuously from his time.

questions.title: How do they fast? Ramadan, Yom Kippur and Lent
questions.asked: What are the rules of fasting in Islam, Judaism and Christianity?
questions.short: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset for the month of Ramadan. Jews fast completely for about 25 hours on Yom Kippur and on a few other days. Christian fasting is mostly abstaining from certain foods, strictest among the Orthodox.

body: **Islam:** a full month of fasting from dawn to sunset, no food, drink or sex, every year. One of the five pillars.
**Judaism:** Yom Kippur is a total fast of about 25 hours, sunset to nightfall; Tisha B'Av is another; several minor fasts run dawn to dusk.
**Christianity:** Lent, forty days before Easter, plus weekly fast days; rules range from strict (Orthodox) to optional (most Protestants).
The Quran itself links them: “Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you” (Quran 2:183).

Ramadan is the month “in which was revealed the Qur'an” (Quran 2:185). The fast runs until the night, and eating, drinking and marital relations are allowed after sunset (Quran 2:187). The sick and travellers make up the days later, and those who cannot fast at all feed a poor person instead (Quran 2:184). Children, the very old, and women who are menstruating or recovering from childbirth do not fast.

Muhammad taught that the fast is about conduct as well as food: “Whoever does not give up forged speech and evil actions, Allah is not in need of his leaving his food and drink” (Sahih al-Bukhari 1903). He also fasted on Ashura after seeing Jews in Medina fast that day for Moses (Sahih al-Bukhari 2004). Shia Muslims keep Ashura as a day of mourning for Husayn.

On the tenth day of the seventh month “you shall afflict your souls” (Leviticus 16:29–31). The rabbis defined affliction as five prohibitions: eating and drinking, bathing, anointing, wearing leather shoes, and marital relations (Mishnah Yoma 8:1). The sick and anyone whose life might be at risk must eat.
Other fasts commemorate the destruction of Jerusalem (Zechariah 8:19) and Esther's three-day fast (Esther 4:16). The prophets warn that fasting without justice is worthless (Isaiah 58:3–7).

Jesus fasted forty days in the desert (Matthew 4:2), taught his followers to fast in secret (Matthew 6:16–18), and said they would fast after he was taken away (Mark 2:18–20). The early church fasted before decisions (Acts 13:2–3).

The Orthodox fast is the strictest in Christianity: on fast days no meat, dairy, eggs, fish (with exceptions), wine or oil. With Lent, three other fasting seasons and most Wednesdays and Fridays, observant Orthodox fast on around half the days of the year.
Catholics today must fast (one full meal and two small ones) on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain from meat on Fridays of Lent. Many give something up for the whole of Lent.
Most Protestant churches have no required fasts. Some observe Lent; many evangelicals fast voluntarily for prayer.
Doctors note risks of long daytime fasts for diabetics and pregnant women, though all three traditions exempt the sick. Some observers point out that Ramadan nights often bring more eating, not less.

questions.title: What do they teach about charity?
questions.asked: What is zakat? Do Christians have to tithe? What is tzedakah?
questions.short: Islam makes zakat, usually 2.5 per cent of savings each year, a compulsory pillar. Judaism treats tzedakah as a legal duty, traditionally a tenth of income. Christianity commands generosity but most churches set no compulsory amount.

body: All three faiths command giving to the poor as a duty, not a favour. Islam and Judaism set minimum amounts in law; Christianity mostly leaves the amount to the giver. The Hebrew word tzedakah means righteousness or justice, not merely charity.

Zakat is paired with prayer throughout the Quran (“Establish worship, pay the poor-due”, Quran 2:43), and the Quran lists who may receive it: the poor, the needy, its collectors, those whose hearts are to be won over, captives, debtors, the cause of God and travellers (Quran 9:60). It purifies wealth (Quran 9:103).

The rate comes from hadith: on silver “the Zakat is one-fortieth” (Sahih al-Bukhari 1454), with separate rates for livestock and crops, and nothing below a minimum threshold. Voluntary giving (sadaqa) is also praised, better given in secret (Quran 2:271), and must not be spoiled by reminding people of it (Quran 2:262–264).
Shia Muslims also pay khums, a fifth of certain surplus income, part of it to the descendants of Muhammad through their religious authorities.

The Torah commands farmers to leave the corners of the field and the gleanings for the poor and the stranger (Leviticus 19:9–10) and forbids hardening your heart against a poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:7–11). The Talmud set a guideline of a tenth of income and capped it: “one who dispenses his money to charity should not dispense more than one-fifth” (Ketubot 50a), so as not to become poor oneself.
Maimonides ranked eight levels of giving; the highest is helping someone become self-supporting.

Jesus tells his followers to give in secret (Matthew 6:1–4) and praises the widow who gave two small coins, “all that she had to live on” (Mark 12:41–44). The first Jerusalem believers held goods in common (Acts 2:44–45). Paul asks each to give “as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Whether Christians must tithe is disputed. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches teach a tenth from Malachi 3:10; Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline churches ask for generous support without a fixed figure. Some Protestants argue the tithe belonged to the Mosaic law and is not binding.

Critics point to abuses: prosperity preachers promising wealth in return for tithes, and in some Muslim states zakat or khums funds controlled by the government or clergy. Defenders say these are abuses of a sound duty.

questions.title: Why Saturday, Sunday or Friday? The Sabbath and holy days
questions.asked: What is the Sabbath? Why do Christians worship on Sunday and Muslims on Friday?
questions.short: The Sabbath is the seventh day, Saturday, commanded in the Ten Commandments. Most Christians gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection. Muslims pray together on Friday, but Friday is not a day of rest.

body: Only Judaism keeps a full Sabbath rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Christians moved their main worship to Sunday very early. Islam has no Sabbath: it requires a congregational prayer at noon on Friday and lets people work before and after.

God rested on the seventh day and blessed it (Genesis 2:2–3). The commandment is given twice, with two reasons: creation (Exodus 20:8–11) and the release from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It is “a sign between me and you” and breaking it carried the death penalty (Exodus 31:13–17). A man caught gathering sticks on the Sabbath was stoned (Numbers 15:32–36).

The rabbis defined work as thirty-nine categories of labour, from sowing and plowing onward (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). Saving a life overrides the Sabbath: “Desecrate one Shabbat on his behalf so he will observe many” (Yoma 85b).

Jesus clashed with Pharisees over Sabbath healing and said “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). The early church met “on the first day of the week” (Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2), the day of the resurrection, called “the Lord's day” (Revelation 1:10). Paul says no one should judge Christians over a Sabbath day (Colossians 2:16).

Catholics, Orthodox and most Protestants keep Sunday. Some Reformed and Presbyterian churches treat Sunday as the Christian Sabbath with strict rest. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists worship on Saturday, arguing that no verse transfers the Sabbath. The Roman emperor Constantine made Sunday a legal day of rest in AD 321.

“When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading. And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land” (Quran 62:9–10). The Quran insists God felt no weariness after creation (Quran 50:38), implicitly rejecting the idea that God rested.

It says the Sabbath was imposed only on those who differed over it (Quran 16:124), and that Sabbath-breakers were told “Be ye apes, despised” (Quran 2:65). Muhammad said Friday was given to Muslims, with Saturday for Jews and Sunday for Christians (Sahih al-Bukhari 876). Friday prayer is obligatory for adult men; Shia jurists long debated whether it is obligatory while the Hidden Imam is absent.

Critics of all three traditions point to the death penalty for Sabbath-breaking in Exodus and Numbers. Jews reply that rabbinic law made capital punishment almost impossible to carry out, and no Jewish court has imposed it for two thousand years.

questions.title: Who wrote the Torah?
questions.asked: Did Moses really write the first five books of the Bible?
questions.short: Jewish and Christian tradition says Moses wrote it, except perhaps the last verses about his death. Most modern scholars think it was compiled from several sources over centuries and reached its final form after the Babylonian exile.

body: The Torah never says who wrote all of it. It says Moses wrote certain laws and songs (Exodus 24:4, Deuteronomy 31:9, Deuteronomy 31:24) and describes him in the third person. It also records his death and burial and says “no man knows where his tomb is to this day” (Deuteronomy 34:5–6).
Tradition credited Moses with the whole; critical scholarship credits multiple authors and editors.

The Talmud says “Moses wrote his own book… and Job. Joshua wrote his own book and eight verses in the Torah”, the verses describing Moses' death (Bava Batra 14b), and records a dissenting opinion that Moses wrote even those with tears (Bava Batra 15a). Denying that the Torah is from Heaven costs a person his share in the World to Come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). Maimonides made the divine origin of the whole Torah one of his thirteen principles.
Orthodox Judaism holds to this. Conservative and Reform Judaism largely accept critical scholarship and see the Torah as inspired but humanly written.

Jesus refers to “the book of Moses” (Mark 12:26) and says Moses “wrote about me” (John 5:46), and the Gospels speak of “the law of Moses” (Luke 24:44). Conservative Protestants take this as confirming Mosaic authorship. The Catholic Church since the mid-20th century allows scholars to study the Torah's sources, while holding that it is inspired; most mainline Protestant scholars accept the source theory.

The Quran says God revealed the Tawrat to Moses (Quran 5:44, Quran 3:3). Many Muslims hold that the present Torah is not identical to what was revealed and point to the account of Moses' death and to the critical scholarship as evidence of later human hands. See [[q/has-the-bible-been-changed|Has the Bible been changed?]].

Medieval Jewish commentators already noticed problems. Abraham ibn Ezra hinted at verses that seem to be written after Moses, such as “At that time, Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6) and the kings of Edom who reigned “before any king reigned over the children of Israel” (Genesis 36:31). Readers also ask how Moses could write that he was “very humble, more than all the men” on earth (Numbers 12:3).

In the 19th century Julius Wellhausen proposed the documentary hypothesis: four sources (J, E, D and P) combined over centuries. Today many scholars have replaced the four neat documents with more complex models, but almost all agree on multiple authors and a final edition in the Persian period, about the 5th century BC.

questions.title: Who wrote the Quran and how was it compiled?
questions.asked: Did Muhammad write the Quran? How was it put together into a book?
questions.short: Muslims believe the Quran is the word of God, recited by Muhammad over about 23 years. It was gathered into a written collection under Abu Bakr and standardised under the caliph Uthman, who had other copies burnt.

body: Muslims hold that Muhammad did not author the Quran: the angel Gabriel delivered it and he recited it. It came in parts over about 23 years (Quran 17:106, Quran 25:32), was memorised and written on scattered materials, collected after his death, and fixed in one official text under Uthman around AD 650.

The first revelation was “Read: In the name of thy Lord” in the cave of Hira (Quran 96:1–5). Muhammad is called the prophet who could neither read nor write (Quran 7:157), which Muslims see as proof the text is not his own (Quran 29:48). The Quran challenges doubters to produce a surah like it (Quran 2:23).

Sahih al-Bukhari records the process. After many reciters were killed at the battle of Yamama, Umar urged Abu Bakr to collect the Quran, and Zayd ibn Thabit gathered it from palm stalks, thin white stones “and also from the men who knew it by heart” (Sahih al-Bukhari 4986). Under Uthman, alarmed by differences in recitation, a committee made copies in the dialect of Quraysh, sent them to the provinces, and ordered “all the other Qur'anic materials… be burnt” (Sahih al-Bukhari 4987). Zayd reports one verse he found only with a single companion (Sahih al-Bukhari 4988).
Muhammad also approved different ways of reciting the same surah (Sahih al-Bukhari 4992), the origin of the recognised readings. This site shows several, such as Hafs and Warsh.

Shia Muslims use the same Uthmanic text. Some early Shia reports claimed that verses about Ali had been removed; leading modern Shia scholars such as Abu al-Qasim al-Khoei rejected this, and mainstream Shia teaching holds that the Quran is complete.

Critics point to hadith in Sunni collections that describe material not in the present Quran. Umar said the verse of stoning for adultery “was revealed… and we did recite this Verse” (Sahih al-Bukhari 6830). Aisha said verses on stoning and on breastfeeding an adult were on a sheet under her pillow that a sheep ate after Muhammad died (Sunan Ibn Majah 1944; its authenticity is disputed), and that a verse on ten sucklings was abrogated by five (Sahih Muslim 1452). Muslims answer that these are abrogated verses (Quran 2:106), withdrawn by God, not lost text.

Manuscript evidence is early. The Birmingham fragments are radiocarbon-dated to roughly AD 568–645, and the Sanaa palimpsest has an erased lower text with small variants from the Uthmanic one, which scholars take as evidence of non-Uthmanic copies before standardisation. Revisionist scholars once argued the Quran took shape over two centuries; the early manuscripts have made that view rare.

questions.title: What is the Talmud?
questions.asked: What is the Talmud and do Jews follow it instead of the Bible?
questions.short: The Talmud is the vast record of rabbinic debate on Jewish law and lore, built around the Mishnah. Rabbinic Judaism treats it as the authoritative interpretation of the Torah, not a replacement for it.

body: The Talmud has two layers. The Mishnah, edited by Rabbi Judah the Prince around AD 200, sets out Jewish law in short rulings. The Gemara is centuries of discussion of the Mishnah by later rabbis. There are two Talmuds: the Jerusalem Talmud (about AD 400) and the larger Babylonian Talmud (about AD 500–600), which is the one normally meant.
It is mostly argument: majority and minority opinions are both recorded, alongside stories, medicine, folklore and ethics.

Rabbinic Judaism holds that Moses received an Oral Torah at Sinai alongside the written one: “Moses received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and the elders to the prophets” (Mishnah Avot 1:1). The Talmud is that oral tradition written down. Without it, many Torah laws cannot be practised; the Torah forbids work on the Sabbath, for example, but never defines work.
Disagreement is built in. Of the schools of Hillel and Shammai a heavenly voice declares “both these and those are the words of the living God” (Eruvin 13b).

Orthodox Jews regard Talmudic law as binding. Conservative Judaism treats it as authoritative but developing. Reform Judaism treats it as a source of guidance, not binding law. Karaite Jews reject it entirely and follow the written Torah alone.

Christians do not regard the Talmud as authoritative. Jesus criticised Pharisees who “set aside the commandment of God… that you may keep your tradition” (Mark 7:8–13). Scholars still study it for the Jewish background of the New Testament. In medieval Europe the Church put the Talmud on trial and burned copies, as in Paris in 1242.

The Quran's statement that whoever kills a soul is as if he killed all mankind is introduced with “We decreed for the Children of Israel” (Quran 5:32). It closely matches a teaching in the Mishnah that one who destroys a single life is considered as if he destroyed an entire world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). Some manuscripts of that Mishnah, including the edition on this site, read “a single life from the Jewish people”.

The Talmud contains hostile passages about Jesus, for example a story that he is punished in the afterlife “with boiling excrement” (Gittin 57a), and a passage on the execution of Yeshu on Passover eve (Sanhedrin 43a). These are real.
Many “Talmud quotes” circulating online, however, are fabricated or badly distorted. Check any quotation against the text itself, which this site provides.

questions.title: Why don't Jews believe in Jesus?
questions.asked: Jesus was Jewish, so why don't Jews accept him as the Messiah or as God?
questions.short: Judaism rejects Jesus on two grounds: he did not do what the prophets said the Messiah would do, and the Christian claim that he is God contradicts Judaism's teaching that God is one and not a man.

body: Jesus and all his first followers were Jews, and Jews of his time disagreed about him from the start. The Jewish case against Christian claims has two parts. First, the Messiah in the prophets is a human king who rebuilds the Temple, gathers the exiles and brings world peace, and the world is not at peace. Second, worshipping a man as God breaks the core of Jewish faith.
The argument over specific prophecies is covered in [[q/is-jesus-the-messiah-of-the-prophets|Is Jesus the Messiah foretold by the prophets?]].

**The Messianic tasks.** The prophets expect the Messiah to gather Israel from the nations (Ezekiel 37:21), reign as a descendant of David with his people living in their land (Ezekiel 37:24–28, Jeremiah 23:5–6), and bring an age when nations “beat their swords into plowshares” and the earth is “full of the knowledge of Yahweh” (Isaiah 2:4, Isaiah 11:9). Maimonides wrote that someone who fails to accomplish these is not the Messiah. Judaism has no second coming to finish the work.

**God is not a man.** “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). “I am God, and not man” (Hosea 11:9). Israel saw no form at Sinai and is forbidden to worship any (Deuteronomy 4:15–16). The incarnation and the Trinity are, in mainstream Jewish thought, incompatible with this.

**The Torah is permanent.** A prophet who leads people away from God's commands is to be rejected even if he performs signs (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Christianity's setting aside of kosher laws, circumcision and the Sabbath for non-Jews is seen as exactly that.
**Translation.** The proof texts often rest on translations Jews dispute, above all “virgin” for the Hebrew almah (young woman) in Isaiah 7:14.
History also weighs heavily: centuries of persecution in Jesus' name, often justified by “May his blood be on us and on our children!” (Matthew 27:25), made the question more than theological.

Christians answer that the prophets also foretold a suffering servant (Isaiah 53:3–5), that the Messiah's reign begins with his first coming and is completed at his return, and that the New Testament writers, all Jews, saw Jesus as fulfilling the Torah rather than abolishing it (Matthew 5:17–18). Paul says a partial hardening has come on Israel “until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26).
Messianic Jews believe in Jesus while keeping Jewish identity and practice; mainstream Jewish bodies of every denomination do not regard them as practising Judaism.

Islam agrees with Christians against Jews that Jesus was the Messiah and was born of a virgin, and agrees with Jews against Christians that he was not God. The Quran criticises those who say “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary” (Quran 5:72) and records Jesus announcing a messenger after him (Quran 61:6).

Historians note that the split took several generations. Jewish followers of Jesus continued in synagogues for decades, and the break hardened after the destruction of the Temple in AD 70 and the Bar Kokhba revolt of AD 132–135, when many Jews followed a different messianic claimant.

questions.title: Is Allah the same God as the God of the Bible?
questions.asked: Do Muslims, Christians and Jews worship the same God?
questions.short: Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, used by Arab Christians and Jews too. The Quran says Muslims worship the same God as Jews and Christians. Whether that is true is disputed within each faith, because they describe God differently.

body: Linguistically, yes: Allah is the Arabic for God, related to the Hebrew Elohim and Aramaic Alaha, and Arabic Bibles use it. Theologically, it depends on whether worshipping the same God requires the same description of him. All three agree God is the creator of everything and the God of Abraham and Moses. Christians add that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, which Islam and Judaism deny.

The Quran tells Muslims to say to the People of the Book: “We believe in that which hath been revealed unto us and revealed unto you; our Allah and your Allah is One” (Quran 29:46). Muslims believe in what was revealed to Abraham, Moses and Jesus (Quran 2:136) and invite Jews and Christians to agree “that we shall worship none but Allah” (Quran 3:64).

The Quran also says Christians who call God “the third of three” disbelieve (Quran 5:73), and accuses some Jews of calling Ezra the son of God (Quran 9:30). So Islam holds it is the same God, wrongly described by others.

Christians are divided. The Catholic Church at the Second Vatican Council (Lumen Gentium 16, Nostra Aetate 3) said Muslims “together with us adore the one, merciful God”. Many Orthodox and mainline Protestants say something similar, while stressing the disagreement over Christ.

Many evangelicals answer no, or only in a limited sense, because Jesus says “No one comes to the Father, except through me” (John 14:6) and “Whoever denies the Son doesn't have the Father” (1 John 2:23). Others note that Jews also deny the Son, yet Christians say Jews worship the God of Abraham. Paul preached to Athenians about the God they worshipped “as unknown” (Acts 17:23).

Medieval Jewish law generally regarded Islam as strict monotheism. Maimonides ruled that a Jew may pray in a mosque but not in a church, because he considered the Trinity and the veneration of images to be forms of idolatry for a Jew. Later authorities treated Christianity more leniently for non-Jews. Deuteronomy 6:4 is the test: Islam's “He is Allah, the One” is close to it.

A popular polemic claims Allah was a pre-Islamic moon god. Pre-Islamic Arabs did know a high god called Allah (Muhammad's father was named Abd Allah, “servant of God”), but scholars find no evidence he was a moon god, and the crescent symbol became associated with Islam only centuries later, under the Ottomans.

questions.title: What is jihad?
questions.asked: Does jihad mean holy war? Is it about inner struggle or fighting?
questions.short: Jihad means striving in God's way. It includes spiritual and moral effort, but in the Quran, hadith and classical Islamic law it very often means armed fighting, both defensive and, in classical law, expansionist.

body: The Arabic word jihad means struggle or effort. The Quran uses it for striving against unbelievers “with the Quran” (Quran 25:52) and for striving in God's path generally (Quran 29:69), and in many verses for fighting (qital). The common claim that jihad is “only inner struggle” is not accurate; the claim that every Muslim is commanded to wage war on non-Muslims is not accurate either.

The first permission to fight was defensive: “Sanction is given unto those who fight because they have been wronged… driven from their homes unjustly” (Quran 22:39–40). “Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities” (Quran 2:190).

Later verses are broader. Quran 9:5 commands killing idolaters after the sacred months, unless they repent and pray, and Quran 9:29 commands fighting People of the Book “until they pay the tribute readily, being brought low”. Hadith say: “I have been ordered to fight against the people until they testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah” (Sahih al-Bukhari 25), and that one who fights “that Allah's Word should be superior” fights in God's cause (Sahih al-Bukhari 2810).

Classical Sunni law developed rules: only legitimate authority declares war, non-combatants such as women and children may not be targeted, and treaties must be kept. It also treated expansionist jihad against non-Muslim lands as a collective duty. Muhammad also said “The best fighting (jihad) in the path of Allah is (to speak) a word of justice to an oppressive ruler” (Sunan Abi Dawud 4344). The saying that inner struggle is the “greater jihad” is widely quoted but is considered weak by hadith scholars.
Most Muslim scholars today hold that jihad as war is legitimate only in defence and condemn terrorism, including attacks on civilians, as forbidden.
In Twelver Shia doctrine, offensive jihad requires the presence of the infallible Imam and is suspended during his occultation; defensive jihad remains a duty.

The Torah commands wars: cities far away are first offered peace (Deuteronomy 20:10–15), but in the cities of Canaan “you shall save alive nothing that breathes” (Deuteronomy 20:16–17). The Talmud distinguishes obligatory wars, like Joshua's conquest, from optional wars of expansion under the kings (Sotah 44b). Rabbinic Judaism regards the Canaanite commands as no longer applicable, since those nations no longer exist.

Jesus told Peter “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). The New Testament has no command to fight for the faith. From Augustine onward most churches accepted a just war theory, and popes proclaimed the Crusades with promises of spiritual reward, which critics regard as a Christian holy war.

Critics point out that groups such as ISIS quote Quran 9:5, Quran 9:29 and classical jurists accurately, and that mainstream scholars must argue those rulings belonged to their time. Muslims answer that the verses have a context of war with specific enemies, and that the Bible contains harsher commands (1 Samuel 15:3).

questions.title: Are angels and jinn real?
questions.asked: What do Christianity, Islam and Judaism teach about angels, demons and jinn?
questions.short: All three faiths teach that angels exist as God's messengers. Islam adds the jinn, beings made of fire who can believe or disbelieve. Christianity and Judaism have demons but no jinn.

body: Angels appear in all three scriptures, and Gabriel and Michael are named in the Bible and the Quran. Belief in angels is one of Islam's six articles of faith. The jinn are distinctly Islamic, though the Talmud has its own demons (shedim).

Muhammad said: “The Angels were born out of light and the Jinns were born out of the spark of fire and Adam was born as he has been defined” (Sahih Muslim 2996). The Quran says the jinn were created “of smokeless fire” (Quran 55:15) before humans (Quran 15:27), and that both were created “only that they might worship Me” (Quran 51:56).

Angels obey and have no free will in mainstream Sunni teaching. Gabriel brought the revelation (Quran 2:97–98); two recording angels sit on each person's right and left (Quran 50:17–18). Jinn are free like humans: some heard the Quran and believed (Quran 72:1–2), others are devils. Iblis, Satan, was of the jinn (Quran 18:50). Belief in possession by jinn and in exorcism (ruqya) is widespread.

Angels are “serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). Gabriel announces Jesus' birth (Luke 1:26), Michael is an archangel who fights the devil (Daniel 10:13, Jude 1:9), and Jesus speaks of children's angels who see God's face (Matthew 18:10), the root of belief in guardian angels.

Demons are understood as fallen angels who followed Satan. Catholic and Orthodox churches keep formal rites of exorcism; Pentecostal churches practise deliverance prayer. Christianity has no concept of jinn.

The Hebrew Bible has angels from Jacob's ladder (Genesis 28:12) to Daniel's named angels, and promises “he will put his angels in charge of you” (Psalm 91:11). The Talmud also describes demons: “Each and every one of us has a thousand demons to his left and ten thousand to his right” (Berakhot 6a).
Maimonides interpreted many angel stories as prophetic visions or natural forces. Many modern Jews take angels symbolically; Kabbalistic and Hasidic Judaism keep a rich angelology.

Historians note that named angels and organised demon armies appear in Judaism mainly after the exile, possibly influenced by Persian religion, and that the jinn were part of pre-Islamic Arabian belief which the Quran absorbed and reshaped. Skeptics see no evidence for any of these beings; believers reply that spiritual beings are not open to physical tests.

questions.title: Who is Satan? The devil and Iblis
questions.asked: Is Satan a fallen angel? Who is Iblis in Islam? Do Jews believe in the devil?
questions.short: In Christianity Satan is a fallen angel and God's chief enemy. In Islam Iblis is a jinn who refused to bow to Adam. In Judaism the satan is mostly an accuser who works under God's authority, not an independent rebel.

body: The Hebrew word satan means adversary or accuser. All three faiths have a figure who tempts humans, but they differ on what he is and how much power he has. Genesis never calls the serpent in Eden Satan (Genesis 3:1); that identification comes later. The Quran names Satan as the tempter of Adam (Quran 20:120).

In Job the satan is one of God's court, who needs God's permission to test Job (Job 1:6–12). In Zechariah he accuses the high priest and is rebuked (Zechariah 3:1–2). Even an angel of God can be “a satan” in someone's way (Numbers 22:22).

The Talmud says: “Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death are one” (Bava Batra 16a). Mainstream Judaism does not teach a devil in rebellion against God; the main struggle is with one's own evil inclination (yetzer hara).

The New Testament makes Satan a personal enemy: “the old serpent, he who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9), “a murderer from the beginning” and “the father of lies” (John 8:44), prowling “like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5:8). Jesus resists his temptations (Matthew 4:1–11) and says “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

Tradition reads Isaiah 14:12, “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one”, as Satan's fall; “Lucifer” comes from the Latin translation of this verse. In context the verse addresses the king of Babylon. All mainstream churches teach that Satan is a created angel who fell through pride, defeated by Christ's cross, and doomed at the end (Revelation 20:10).

When God commanded the angels to bow to Adam, “they fell prostrate, all save Iblis. He demurred through pride” (Quran 2:34). He argued “I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud” (Quran 7:11–18), and was given respite until the Day of Judgment to mislead people, though he has no power over God's sincere servants (Quran 15:39–42). On that day he will disown his followers: “I had no power over you save that I called unto you and ye obeyed me” (Quran 14:22).

Muslims debate whether Iblis was an angel or a jinn; Quran 18:50 says “He was of the jinn”. Hadith say Satan “reaches everywhere in the human body as blood reaches in it” (Sahih al-Bukhari 2035) and that yawning is from Satan (Sahih al-Bukhari 3289).

Historians trace the growth of the devil from the accuser of Job to the cosmic enemy of the New Testament, with Persian dualism and Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch as likely influences. Skeptics note that a devil explains evil only by moving the question back: why did God create him?

questions.title: What are the Ten Commandments in each faith?
questions.asked: Do Christians, Jews and Muslims have the same Ten Commandments?
questions.short: Jews and Christians share the Ten Commandments of Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 but number them differently. The Quran has no list of ten, but Quran 6:151–153 and 17:22–39 contain most of the same commands.

body: The Bible gives the commandments twice, in Exodus 20:2–17 and Deuteronomy 5:6–21, with small differences. The Hebrew text calls them “the ten words” (Exodus 34:28) but never numbers them, so different traditions divide the text differently.
**Jewish:** 1 “I am Yahweh your God”; 2 no other gods and no idols; then the name, Sabbath, parents, murder, adultery, stealing, false witness, coveting.
**Catholic and Lutheran** (following Augustine): 1 no other gods (including the ban on images); coveting is split into two, neighbour's wife and neighbour's goods.
**Orthodox and Reformed** (following Philo and Origen): 1 no other gods; 2 no images; coveting is one.

For Judaism the Ten are not a summary of the law; they are part of 613 commandments: “There were 613 mitzvot stated to Moses” (Makkot 23b). The Ten were once recited daily in the Temple, but the rabbis stopped the practice outside it “due to the grievance of the heretics”, who claimed only the Ten were given at Sinai (Berakhot 12a). The first “commandment” is a statement of belief: “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”.

Jesus lists several when asked how to gain eternal life (Matthew 19:17–19) and sums up the law as love of God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40); Paul does the same (Romans 13:9). Christians treat the Ten as the moral law still in force, but most observe Sunday rather than the seventh-day Sabbath of the fourth commandment, which they see as fulfilled in Christ.

The numbering matters in practice: Reformed churches, counting images as a separate commandment, historically removed statues and pictures from churches. Catholics and Orthodox use images and say the ban was on worshipping them as gods.

The Quran says God wrote for Moses “upon the tablets” guidance in all things (Quran 7:145). It has no numbered decalogue, but Quran 6:151–153 lists: ascribe no partner to God, be good to parents, do not kill your children for fear of poverty, avoid lewdness, do not kill except by right, do not touch the orphan's wealth, give full measure, speak justly, and keep God's covenant. Quran 17:22–39 is a longer parallel.
Missing from both Quranic lists is the Sabbath, which the Quran treats as a law for Jews only.

Scholars note that Exodus 34 contains a different set of commands, mostly about festivals and sacrifices, after which the text says Moses wrote “the ten words” (Exodus 34:28). Critics also point out that the commandment on coveting lists a wife among a man's possessions.

questions.title: Can women be priests, imams or rabbis?
questions.asked: Are women allowed to lead prayer or be clergy in Christianity, Islam and Judaism?
questions.short: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity and Orthodox Judaism ordain only men; mainstream Islam does not allow women to lead mixed congregations in prayer. Many Protestant churches and Reform and Conservative Judaism ordain women.

body: The oldest and largest branches of all three faiths reserve the main leadership role for men. All three scriptures nevertheless include women prophets or teachers: Deborah judged Israel (Judges 4:4), the prophetess Huldah was consulted by the king's officials (2 Kings 22:14), Philip had four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9), and Aisha was one of the most important early teachers of Islam.

The main texts against women leaders are Paul's: “I don't permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:11–12), and “Let the wives be quiet in the assemblies” (1 Corinthians 14:34–35). The main texts the other way are Phoebe, “a servant [diakonos] of the assembly” (Romans 16:1), Junia, “notable among the apostles” (Romans 16:7), and “there is neither male nor female… in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

The Catholic Church teaches that it has no authority to ordain women as priests, because Christ chose only men as apostles; Pope John Paul II declared this definitive in 1994 (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis). Women can be lay ministers and lead religious orders.
The Orthodox Churches ordain only men as priests and bishops. Women served as deaconesses in the early church, and some Orthodox churches have discussed or begun reviving the order.

Protestants are split. Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and many Pentecostals ordain women, and some have women bishops. The Southern Baptist Convention, conservative Presbyterians and many evangelical churches restrict the role of pastor to men, citing 1 Timothy 2.

The four Sunni schools and Shia jurists agree that a woman may lead other women in prayer but not a congregation of men. Islam has no ordained priesthood, so the question is mainly about leading prayer, preaching and issuing legal opinions. Many women have been respected scholars and teachers.

A hadith says Muhammad told Umm Waraqa “to lead the inmates of her house in prayer” and appointed a muezzin for her (Sunan Abi Dawud 592); a minority argue this included men. Another, “Such people as ruled by a lady will never be successful” (Sahih al-Bukhari 4425), spoken about the Persians crowning a daughter of Khosrau, is cited against women in political leadership. Amina Wadud's leading of a mixed Friday prayer in New York in 2005 was condemned by most scholars.

Women are exempt from many “positive time-bound commandments” (Mishnah Kiddushin 1:7), which was the traditional basis for not counting them in the prayer quorum or having them lead services. Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women as rabbis, though some Modern Orthodox institutions now train women as halakhic advisers.

Regina Jonas was privately ordained in Germany in 1935 and murdered at Auschwitz. Reform Judaism ordained Sally Priesand in 1972, Reconstructionist Judaism followed in 1974 and Conservative Judaism in 1985.

Critics see male-only leadership as discrimination rooted in ancient patriarchy. Traditionalists in all three faiths reply that men and women have different but equal roles, and that the tradition cannot be changed by modern opinion.

questions.title: Do Christians, Muslims and Jews all believe in the virgin birth?
questions.asked: Does the Quran teach that Mary was a virgin? Do Jews believe Jesus was born of a virgin?
questions.short: Christianity and Islam both teach that Jesus was born of the virgin Mary without a human father. Judaism does not, and reads the key prophecy, Isaiah 7:14, as speaking of a young woman in the prophet's own day.

body: Yes for Christians and Muslims, no for Jews. The Quran affirms the virgin birth as clearly as the Gospels, though it denies that it makes Jesus the Son of God. Mary is the only woman named in the Quran, and a whole surah carries her name.

Matthew says Mary “was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit” before she and Joseph came together, and that Joseph “didn't know her sexually until she had given birth” (Matthew 1:18–25). In Luke, Mary asks “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?” and is told “The Holy Spirit will come on you” (Luke 1:34–35). Matthew sees it as fulfilling Isaiah 7:14 in its Greek form, “the virgin will conceive”. The virgin birth is in both the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians also believe Mary remained a virgin all her life, and read the “brothers” of Jesus (Mark 6:3) as cousins or Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. Catholics further teach the Immaculate Conception, that Mary herself was conceived without original sin; the Orthodox do not accept that dogma.

Most Protestants accept the virgin birth but read Mark 6:3 and Matthew 1:25 to mean Mary had other children with Joseph after Jesus. Some liberal Protestant theologians treat the virgin birth as symbolic.

The angels tell Mary she will have a son, and she answers “My Lord! How can I have a child when no mortal hath touched me?” God replies that He creates what He wills by saying “Be!” (Quran 3:45–47). Surah 19 tells how God's Spirit appeared to her as a man and announced a pure son (Quran 19:16–22). God “breathed into her (something) of Our Spirit” (Quran 21:91, Quran 66:12).

The Quran explains the miracle without making Jesus divine: “the likeness of Jesus with Allah is as the likeness of Adam. He created him of dust” (Quran 3:59). Mary is chosen “above (all) the women of creation” (Quran 3:42). See also [[q/mary-and-jesus-in-the-quran|Does the Quran get Mary and Jesus wrong?]]

Judaism does not believe Jesus was born of a virgin. The Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 has almah, a young woman, not betulah, the usual word for virgin, and the sign is for King Ahaz: before the child is old enough to choose good, the two kings threatening him will be gone (Isaiah 7:16). Jewish tradition also expects the Messiah to be a descendant of David through his father, which a virgin birth would complicate. Medieval Jewish polemic, such as the Toledot Yeshu, told hostile alternative stories of Jesus' birth.

Historians note that the earliest New Testament writers do not mention the virgin birth: Paul says only that Jesus was “born to a woman” (Galatians 4:4), and Mark begins with Jesus as an adult. Matthew and Luke tell different birth stories and give different genealogies through Joseph (Matthew 1:16, Luke 3:23). Skeptics compare the story to miraculous births of heroes in Greek and Roman legend; believers answer that those stories involve gods physically fathering children, which the Gospels do not describe.

questions.title: Who was Abraham?
questions.asked: Why is Abraham important to Judaism, Christianity and Islam?
questions.short: Abraham is the founding figure of all three faiths, which are often called Abrahamic. Jews see him as the father of their nation and covenant, Christians as the model of faith, and Muslims as a prophet who built the Kaaba and was neither Jew nor Christian.

body: In Genesis God calls Abram to leave his country and promises “I will make of you a great nation… All the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:1–3). He has two sons, Ishmael by Hagar and Isaac by Sarah (Genesis 16:15, Genesis 21:2–3), and both bury him (Genesis 25:9). Jews trace descent through Isaac, Arabs traditionally through Ishmael. Which son he nearly sacrificed is covered in [[q/isaac-or-ishmael|Isaac or Ishmael?]].

Abraham is “our father”, the first to make the covenant with God, sealed by circumcision, and the first of the three patriarchs. “With ten trials was Abraham, our father… tried, and he withstood them all” (Mishnah Avot 5:3). A famous midrash, not in the Bible, tells of him smashing the idols in his father Terah's shop; the Bible says only that Terah's family “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2). Converts to Judaism take the name “son” or “daughter of Abraham”.

For Paul, Abraham proves that righteousness comes by faith: “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness” (Romans 4:3, quoting Genesis 15:6), before he was circumcised (Romans 4:11). So all who believe are Abraham's children (Galatians 3:6–9). James uses Abraham's offering of Isaac to show that faith works (James 2:21–23). Jesus says “before Abraham came into existence, I AM” (John 8:58), which Christians read as a claim to divinity.

Ibrahim is one of the greatest prophets and “friend” of God (Quran 4:125). “Abraham was not a Jew, nor yet a Christian; but he was an upright man who had surrendered (to Allah)” (Quran 3:67), so Muslims see Islam as the restoration of his religion. The Quran tells how he broke his people's idols and was thrown into a fire that God made cool (Quran 21:51–70).

With Ishmael he raised the foundations of the Kaaba in Mecca (Quran 2:125–127), and he was told to proclaim the pilgrimage (Quran 22:27). The Quran mentions scriptures of Abraham (Quran 87:19), which do not survive. Muslims pray for Abraham and his family in every prayer.

There is no archaeological or outside evidence that Abraham existed, and many historians treat the stories as national traditions written down centuries later. They point to details such as domesticated camels (Genesis 24:10), which were not common in the region until around the 10th century BC, as later colouring. Conservative scholars argue the stories fit the second millennium BC in other respects. Historians also find no evidence before the Quran linking Abraham to Mecca.

questions.title: Is music allowed?
questions.asked: Is music haram in Islam? Do Jews and Christians allow musical instruments?
questions.short: Music is a contested question only in Islam, where many scholars forbid musical instruments based on hadith while others allow them. Judaism and Christianity have used music in worship from the start, though some groups avoid instruments.

body: The Quran does not mention music explicitly. The debate in Islam is over hadith. The Hebrew Bible is full of music: “Praise him with harp and lyre!” (Psalm 150:3–5). Rabbinic Judaism restricted it after the Temple's destruction, and some Christian churches sing without instruments.

The strongest text against music is a hadith in which Muhammad warns of people who “will consider illegal sexual intercourse, the wearing of silk, the drinking of alcoholic drinks and the use of musical instruments, as lawful” (Sahih al-Bukhari 5590). Ibn Mas'ud and others interpreted the “pastime of discourse” used to mislead from God's way (Quran 31:6) as singing.

On the other side, when two girls sang on the day of Eid in Aisha's house and Abu Bakr protested “Musical instruments of Satan”, Muhammad said “There is an `Id for every nation and this is our `Id” (Sahih al-Bukhari 952). The daff (frame drum) is widely accepted at weddings.

Most classical Sunni scholars forbade stringed and wind instruments, while allowing unaccompanied singing with decent words. A minority, including Ibn Hazm, questioned the hadith's chain and allowed music. Sufi orders made music and chant (sama) part of worship. Shia jurists generally prohibit ghina, entertaining singing, though they define it differently. Today many Muslims listen to music; Salafi scholars usually forbid it.

The Levites sang with harps, lyres and cymbals in the Temple (1 Chronicles 15:16). After its destruction the rabbis restricted music as a sign of mourning: the Talmud asks how we know “song is forbidden” today and cites “Rejoice not, O Israel” (Gittin 7a), and says that when the Sanhedrin ceased, song ceased at feasts (Sotah 48a). In practice later law limited this, and singing is central to Jewish prayer and Sabbath meals. Orthodox Jews do not play instruments on the Sabbath; many Reform synagogues use organs.

Paul tells Christians to speak “in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19). Music has been central to Christian worship. Orthodox churches use only unaccompanied voices in the liturgy, the Churches of Christ sing a cappella, and early Reformed churches sang only psalms without instruments. No major church forbids music outside worship.

Critics of strict Islamic positions point to bans on music by the Taliban and ISIS. Defenders of the ban say it concerns morally corrupting entertainment, not sound itself, and that it is held by the majority of classical scholars.

questions.title: Why do some Muslims, Jews and Christians cover their heads?
questions.asked: Is the hijab required in the Quran? Why do Jewish men wear a kippah? Should Christian women wear veils?
questions.short: The Quran tells women to cover their bosoms with their khimar and draw their cloaks around them; most scholars take this to require covering the hair. The Jewish kippah is a custom, not a Torah law. Paul tells Christian women to cover their heads in worship, a practice most churches have dropped.

body: All three traditions have rules on covering, but they rest on different texts and are kept by very different shares of believers. The word hijab in the Quran means a screen or curtain, not a headscarf (Quran 33:53).

The Quran tells believing women to lower their gaze and “to display of their adornment only that which is apparent, and to draw their veils over their bosoms” (Quran 24:31), and tells the Prophet's wives, daughters and believing women “to draw their cloaks close round them… so that they may be recognised and not annoyed” (Quran 33:59). The Arabic khimar was a head covering, so the four Sunni schools and Shia jurists hold that covering the hair is obligatory for adult women in front of unrelated men.

Scholars differ over the face. A hadith says that once a woman reaches puberty nothing should be seen “except this and this”, pointing to face and hands (Sunan Abi Dawud 4104), but Abu Dawud himself notes it is mursal, a weak chain. The Hanafi and Maliki schools generally do not require a face veil; some Hanbali and Salafi scholars do. A minority of modern Muslim scholars argue the hijab is not obligatory at all.

No verse in the Torah requires men to cover their heads. The Talmud records it as an act of piety: Rav Huna “would not walk four cubits with an uncovered head. He said: The Divine Presence is above my head” (Kiddushin 31a), and a mother tells her son “Cover your head so that the fear of Heaven will be upon you” (Shabbat 156b). It became universal custom among Orthodox men; many Reform Jews cover their heads only in prayer, or not at all.

Married Orthodox women cover their hair with a scarf, hat or wig. The Talmud derives this from the ritual of the suspected adulteress, whose hair was loosened (Numbers 5:18), and counts going out with an uncovered head as violating the practice of Jewish women (Ketubot 72a).

Paul writes that “every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head” while a man should pray uncovered, but also that a woman's hair “is given to her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:4–16). Readers differ on whether he means a veil or long hair, and whether it was a universal rule or a local custom.

Catholic canon law required women to cover their heads in church until 1983, and some traditional Catholics still wear a mantilla. Many Orthodox women wear headscarves in church. Amish, Mennonite and some other Anabaptist women cover their heads at all times. Most Protestant churches no longer practise it.

Critics argue that covering women but not men reflects control of women's bodies, and point to laws enforcing the hijab in Iran and Afghanistan. Many Muslim women answer that they choose it freely, and that bans on headscarves in some European countries also deny women choice.

questions.title: Why do Jews and Muslims circumcise?
questions.asked: Is circumcision required in Judaism, Islam and Christianity? Is it in the Quran?
questions.short: Circumcision of boys is a Torah commandment and the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. In Islam it is a strongly established practice from hadith, not mentioned in the Quran. The New Testament says Christians do not need it.

body: Judaism circumcises boys on the eighth day as a commandment. Islam circumcises boys as part of the natural way (fitra), at varying ages. Christianity decided at the Council of Jerusalem that non-Jewish believers need not be circumcised, and treats it as a medical or cultural choice.

“This is my covenant… Every male among you shall be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10–14). A boy is circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), and the brit milah is performed even when that day falls on the Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 19:2). It is postponed if the child's health requires. An uncircumcised Jewish man is still Jewish, but has failed to keep the commandment.

Most Jews, including most secular Jews, keep it. A minority of ultra-Orthodox mohels perform metzitzah b'peh, oral suction of the wound, which has caused herpes infections in infants and is controversial within Orthodoxy.

The Quran does not mention circumcision. Hadith list it first among the practices of the fitra: “circumcision, shaving the pubic region, clipping the nails and cutting the moustaches short” (Sahih al-Bukhari 5889), and say Abraham “circumcised himself after he had passed the age of eighty years… with an adze” (Sahih al-Bukhari 6298). The Shafi'i and Hanbali schools make it obligatory for men; the Hanafi and Maliki call it a strongly recommended sunna. Shia jurists hold it obligatory.

Female circumcision is also discussed in classical law. A hadith tells a woman who circumcised girls “Do not cut severely” (Sunan Abi Dawud 5271), but Abu Dawud himself says “It is not a strong tradition.” The Shafi'i school traditionally considered it obligatory; many modern scholars and Al-Azhar have declared female genital mutilation forbidden. It persists in parts of Africa and Asia among Muslims and Christians alike.

Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21). When some taught that converts “can't be saved” unless circumcised (Acts 15:1–2), the apostles decided against requiring it. Paul is blunt: “if you receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5:2–6), “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing” (1 Corinthians 7:18–19), and true circumcision is “of the heart” (Romans 2:28–29). The Coptic and Ethiopian churches still circumcise boys as custom.

Opponents argue that circumcising infants violates bodily autonomy, and some European politicians have proposed bans; Jewish and Muslim groups call such bans an attack on religious freedom. Medical bodies disagree on whether the health benefits justify routine circumcision. Female genital cutting is condemned by the World Health Organization and has no health benefits.

questions.title: What is sin, and how is it forgiven?
questions.asked: How do you get forgiveness in Christianity, Islam and Judaism? What is the unforgivable sin?
questions.short: All three call sin disobedience to God and teach that God forgives the repentant. Christianity says forgiveness comes through Christ's death. Islam and Judaism say God forgives directly through repentance, with no sacrifice needed.

body: The great dividing line is atonement. Christianity teaches that “apart from shedding of blood there is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22) and that Christ's death is the sacrifice for all sin. Judaism, without a Temple since AD 70, teaches that repentance, prayer and good deeds bring forgiveness. Islam teaches that God forgives whom He wills, and no one carries another's sin (Quran 6:164).
The question of inherited sin is covered in [[q/original-sin|Do we inherit Adam's sin?]] and of how salvation is received in [[q/faith-or-works|Faith or works?]].

“All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and “the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:23). “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). The one sin Jesus calls unforgivable is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–29), usually understood as a final, hardened rejection of God.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess serious sins to a priest, citing Jesus' words to the apostles: “If you forgive anyone's sins, they have been forgiven them” (John 20:23). Catholics distinguish mortal sins, which cut off grace, from venial ones, drawing on 1 John 5:16–17.
Protestants confess directly to God and reject the need for a priest's absolution, though Lutherans and Anglicans keep private confession as an option.

“Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins” (Quran 39:53). The exception is shirk, associating partners with God, if one dies without repenting of it: “Allah forgiveth not that a partner should be ascribed unto Him” (Quran 4:48). For those who repent and do good, “Allah will change their evil deeds to good deeds” (Quran 25:70).

Muhammad listed seven “great destructive sins”: shirk, sorcery, unlawful killing, usury, consuming an orphan's wealth, fleeing from battle, and slandering chaste women (Sahih al-Bukhari 2766). He also said that if people did not sin, God would replace them with people who sin and seek forgiveness (Sahih Muslim 2749). Repentance (tawba) is made directly to God; Islam has no confession to clergy. Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet and the Imams were sinless and can intercede.

Judaism has no doctrine of inherited guilt: “The soul who sins, he shall die… if the wicked turns from all his sins… he shall surely live” (Ezekiel 18:20–23). God desires “mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). Psalm 51, David's prayer after Bathsheba, is the model of repentance (teshuvah).

Yom Kippur atones for sins against God, but “for transgressions between a person and another, Yom Kippur does not atone until he appeases the other person” (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). The same passage warns that one who says “I will sin and repent” will not be given the chance.

Jewish and Muslim critics argue that the Christian idea of one man dying for others' sins contradicts Ezekiel 18. Christians answer that Christ is not a third party but God himself bearing the cost. Secular critics object to the idea that wrong belief, such as shirk or rejecting Christ, is the gravest sin of all.

questions.title: Can you marry someone of another faith?
questions.asked: Can a Muslim marry a Christian? Can a Jew marry a non-Jew? What does the Bible say about interfaith marriage?
questions.short: Islam allows a Muslim man to marry a Jewish or Christian woman but forbids a Muslim woman to marry any non-Muslim man. Orthodox Judaism does not recognise marriage to a non-Jew. Christianity discourages it but most churches allow it.

body: The traditional rules of all three faiths aim to keep children in the faith. They are strictest in Judaism, asymmetric between men and women in Islam, and most flexible in Christianity. In all three, practice in the modern West has moved far from the rules.

“The food of those who have received the Scripture is lawful for you… And so are the virtuous women of the believers and the virtuous women of those who received the Scripture before you” (Quran 5:5). Muslims may not marry idolaters, men or women, until they believe (Quran 2:221). Believing women who emigrated “are not lawful for the disbelievers” (Quran 60:10).

From these verses classical Sunni and Shia law agree that a Muslim woman may not marry a non-Muslim man at all; the reasoning is that the husband heads the household and children follow the father's religion. Many Shia jurists permit marriage to Christian or Jewish women only in temporary marriage. A small number of modern scholars argue women should have the same right as men; this remains a minority view.

The Torah forbids marrying the Canaanite nations: “You shall not make marriages with them… for that would turn away your sons from following me” (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). Ezra made returned exiles send away their foreign wives and children (Ezra 10:2–3), and Nehemiah fought mixed marriages (Nehemiah 13:23–27).

Jewish status passes through the mother: the child of a gentile woman “is like her” (Mishnah Kiddushin 3:12). Orthodox and Conservative Judaism do not perform or recognise marriages between a Jew and a non-Jew unless the partner converts. Many Reform rabbis officiate at them, and Reform Judaism since 1983 also recognises children of a Jewish father who are raised Jewish.

Paul tells believers not to be “unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14), and a widow may remarry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). But he also tells Christians already married to unbelievers to stay married, because the unbelieving spouse is “sanctified” by the believer (1 Corinthians 7:12–16).
Catholics may marry an unbaptised person with a dispensation from the bishop for “disparity of cult”, and the Catholic partner promises to do all they can to raise the children Catholic.
Orthodox Churches will marry an Orthodox Christian only to a baptised Christian; marriage to a Muslim or Jew cannot take place in an Orthodox church.

Critics point to the inequality in Islamic law between men and women, and to the pressure on converts in all three faiths. In several Muslim-majority countries the law still forbids a Muslim woman to marry a non-Muslim, and in Israel there is no civil marriage, so interfaith couples must marry abroad.

questions.title: What happens at the end of the world? Antichrist, Dajjal and the Messiah
questions.asked: What do the three faiths teach about the end times, the Antichrist and the Dajjal?
questions.short: Christians expect Jesus to return and defeat the Antichrist. Muslims also expect Jesus to return and kill the Dajjal, the false messiah, alongside the Mahdi. Jews expect the Messiah to come for the first time and bring the resurrection.

body: All three faiths expect history to end with a final deceiver, a saviour, the resurrection and the judgment. Strikingly, both Christians and Muslims expect Jesus to return. All three also warn against setting dates: “no one knows of that day and hour” (Matthew 24:36), “the knowledge of it is with Allah only” (Quran 33:63).
