Jesus foretells signs in the sky and the Son of Man coming on the clouds to gather his elect (Matthew 24:29–31). Paul speaks of “the man of sin… who opposes and exalts himself against all that is called God” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4); John speaks of the Antichrist and of “many antichrists” already present (1 John 2:18). Revelation adds the beast whose mark is needed to buy or sell, numbered 666 (Revelation 13:16–18), and a thousand-year reign (Revelation 20:1–6).

Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches read the thousand years symbolically (amillennialism). Many American evangelicals hold dispensational premillennialism, with a rapture of believers (based on 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), a seven-year tribulation and a literal millennium. The rapture as a separate event is a 19th-century teaching, unknown to the early church.

The Hour is a basic article of faith. Hadith describe the Dajjal: “He is blind in one eye, and your Lord is not so, and there will be written between his eyes (the word) Kafir” (Sahih al-Bukhari 7131). Jesus will descend, “break the Cross and kill the pigs” and abolish the jizya (Sahih al-Bukhari 3448), and will catch the Dajjal “at the gate of Ludd and would kill him” (Sahih Muslim 2937). Muslims read Quran 43:61 and Quran 4:159 as alluding to his return. Gog and Magog will break loose.

Most Sunnis expect the Mahdi, a man from Muhammad's family “whose father's name is the same as my father's, who will fill the earth with equity and justice” (Sunan Abi Dawud 4282), “of the descendants of Fatimah” (Sunan Abi Dawud 4284). He is not mentioned in Bukhari or Muslim, and a minority of Sunni scholars doubt the reports.

For Twelver Shia the Mahdi is the twelfth Imam, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, born in the 9th century, who went into hiding in 874 and is alive in occultation. His return, with Jesus at his side, is central to Shia hope.

Jews await the Messiah's first coming: a king of David's line who gathers the exiles and brings peace, when “the wolf will live with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6–9). Ezekiel foretells a war of Gog of the land of Magog (Ezekiel 38:2). Then the dead will rise (Daniel 12:2).

The Talmud records the teaching that “Six thousand years is the duration of the world” (Sanhedrin 97a), but also curses “those who calculate the end of days” (Sanhedrin 97b). Judaism has no Antichrist figure, though some traditions speak of an evil king called Armilus.

Critics note that Jesus seems to say the end would come within his hearers' lifetime: “this generation will not pass away until all these things happen” (Mark 13:30, Matthew 16:28). Christians answer that he referred to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 or to the kingdom's beginning. In every faith, countless predictions of the end have failed, and apocalyptic belief has fuelled violence, from medieval movements to ISIS's propaganda about Dabiq.

questions.title: Is everything predestined, or do we have free will?
questions.asked: Does God decide everything? What is qadr? Do Christians believe in predestination?
questions.short: All three faiths affirm both that God knows and decrees everything and that humans are responsible for their choices. Each has had schools that pushed hard one way: Calvinists and Ash'aris toward God's decree, Arminians and Mu'tazilites toward human freedom.

body: The Mishnah puts the position shared in some form by all three: “Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted” (Mishnah Avot 3:15). The arguments are about how the two fit together, and whether God chooses who will be saved.

Belief in divine decree (qadar) is one of the six articles of faith. In the hadith of Gabriel, faith includes affirming “the Divine Decree about good and evil” (Sahih Muslim 8). “We have created every thing by measure” (Quran 54:49), and “ye will not, unless Allah willeth” (Quran 76:30). An angel writes each person's provision, lifespan and whether he will be “of the wretched or the blessed” while still in the womb (Sahih al-Bukhari 6594).

The Quran also says “whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve” (Quran 18:29) and “Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts” (Quran 13:11). Early Mu'tazilite theologians stressed human free will to protect God's justice; the Ash'ari school, dominant among Sunnis, taught that God creates all acts and humans “acquire” them. Shia theology follows a saying attributed to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq: “neither compulsion nor complete delegation, but a matter between the two”.

Paul writes “whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Romans 8:29–30), that God “has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires” (Romans 9:18–21), and that God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4–5). Yet God “desires all people to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4) and is “not wishing that anyone should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

Calvinists teach unconditional election: God chooses whom to save, not based on anything foreseen in them, and those he chooses will certainly believe. Luther argued in The Bondage of the Will that the human will cannot choose God unaided. Arminians, including Methodists and many Baptists and Pentecostals, teach that God predestines those he foresees will freely believe.

The Catholic Church teaches predestination to glory but rejects predestination to hell, and affirms that grace and free will cooperate. The Orthodox emphasise synergy, human freedom working with God's grace, and have never adopted Augustine's strong predestinarian views.

“I have set before you life and death… Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19) is the foundation of Jewish teaching on free will. “Everything is in the hands of Heaven, except for fear of Heaven” (Berakhot 33b): God controls circumstances, but moral choice is human. Maimonides made free will a pillar of the Torah. The hardening of Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12) is the classic difficulty, explained as God confirming choices Pharaoh had already made.

Critics argue that if God decrees everything, punishing people for what he decreed is unjust, a charge raised by Muslims against Calvinism and by Christians against Ash'arism. Philosophers note that the same puzzle, foreknowledge versus freedom, exists for any all-knowing God.

questions.title: Who is the Holy Spirit?
questions.asked: Is the Holy Spirit God? Who is the Holy Spirit in Islam and Judaism?
questions.short: For Christians the Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity. In Islam the “holy spirit” is usually identified with the angel Gabriel. In Judaism it is God's spirit or presence, especially the spirit of prophecy, not a separate person.

body: The phrase appears in all three scriptures. The Hebrew Bible speaks of “your Holy Spirit” (Psalm 51:11, Isaiah 63:10) as God's own spirit. The New Testament speaks of the Spirit as someone who teaches and can be lied to. The Quran's ruh al-qudus brought the revelation (Quran 16:102) and supported Jesus (Quran 2:87).

Christians baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Jesus promises “another Counselor… the Spirit of truth” who will teach his disciples (John 14:16–17, John 14:26), and the Spirit comes at Pentecost with wind and tongues of fire (Acts 2:1–4). When Ananias lies “to the Holy Spirit”, Peter says he has lied “to God” (Acts 5:3–4).

The Council of Constantinople in 381 declared the Spirit “the Lord, the giver of life… worshipped and glorified” with the Father and the Son. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians emphasise gifts of the Spirit such as speaking in tongues and healing. See [[q/one-god-or-trinity|One God or Trinity?]]

Jesus says the Spirit “proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). The Western church later added to the creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father “and the Son” (filioque). The Orthodox reject the addition, and it was a central cause of the split of 1054. Most Protestants kept the Western wording.

Most Muslim commentators identify the holy spirit with Gabriel, who “hath delivered it from thy Lord with truth” (Quran 16:102), called the “True Spirit” who brought the Quran down (Quran 26:193). God gave Jesus clear proofs “and We supported him with the holy Spirit” (Quran 2:87). God's Spirit was also breathed into Adam and into Mary. Islam firmly denies that the Spirit is divine.

Many Muslims identify the Counselor promised in John 14 with Muhammad, linking it to Jesus' announcement of “Ahmad” (Quran 61:6). See [[q/is-muhammad-foretold-in-the-bible|Is Muhammad foretold in the Bible?]]

The spirit of God hovers over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), and God promises “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28). In rabbinic Judaism ruach ha-kodesh is the spirit of prophecy and inspiration, not a person. The Talmud says that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died, “the Divine Spirit of prophetic revelation departed from the Jewish people” (Yoma 9b, Sanhedrin 11a).

Historians note that the full doctrine of the Spirit as a distinct divine person was settled only in the 4th century, and that some earlier Christians spoke of the Spirit in ways closer to the Jewish idea of God's power. Christians answer that the doctrine only made explicit what the New Testament already shows.

questions.title: What happens if you leave the faith? Apostasy
questions.asked: Is there a death penalty for leaving Islam? What do Christianity and Judaism say about apostates?
questions.short: Classical Islamic law in all main schools prescribed death for male apostates, based on hadith; many modern Muslim scholars reject this. The Torah prescribes death for those who entice others to worship other gods, but Judaism has not applied it for two thousand years. Christian states once executed heretics; no church teaches that today.

body: All three traditions have, at some point, punished those who abandoned the faith. Today, apostasy is a crime only in some Muslim-majority countries, where it can lead to execution, imprisonment, loss of marriage or inheritance. Christianity and Judaism today treat it as a spiritual matter.

The Quran condemns apostasy severely but names no worldly punishment: whoever disbelieves after believing, except under compulsion, earns God's wrath and “an awful doom” (Quran 16:106); those who die as apostates have their works fail in this world and the next (Quran 2:217). It also says “There is no compulsion in religion” (Quran 2:256).

The death penalty comes from hadith: “Whoever changed his Islamic religion, then kill him” (Sahih al-Bukhari 6922), and a Muslim's blood may be shed in three cases, including “the one who reverts from Islam (apostate) and leaves the Muslims” (Sahih al-Bukhari 6878). The four Sunni schools and Shia law agreed on execution for a sane adult male apostate, usually after a chance to repent; the Hanafi school and Shia law imprison rather than execute a woman.

Many modern scholars argue the hadith concerned treason, deserting the community in wartime, and that Quran 2:256 forbids punishing belief. Others defend the classical ruling, and it remains on the books in several countries.

The Torah commands that a relative or friend who secretly entices others “Let's go and serve other gods” shall be stoned (Deuteronomy 13:6–10). Rabbinic courts surrounded capital cases with near-impossible conditions, and no Jewish court has had capital jurisdiction since Roman times.

In Jewish law a Jew who leaves remains a Jew: from “Israel has sinned” the Talmud infers that “even when the Jewish people have sinned, they are still called Israel” (Sanhedrin 44a). Communities have shunned apostates, and some Orthodox families sit mourning for a child who converts.

The New Testament warns that those who fall away after being enlightened cannot be restored to repentance (Hebrews 6:4–6) and that their last state is worse than the first (2 Peter 2:20–22), but prescribes no human penalty. Calvinists teach that true believers never finally fall away; others hold that salvation can be lost.

From the 4th century onward, Christian rulers made heresy and apostasy crimes. The medieval and Spanish Inquisitions handed people to the state for burning, and Protestant states executed heretics too. No church today supports any civil penalty.

Human rights organisations note that apostasy remains punishable by death in law in a number of countries, including Saudi Arabia, Iran and Afghanistan, and that former Muslims elsewhere face threats from families and communities. Critics of all three faiths argue that the old laws show each religion relied on force; defenders answer that the laws reflect the merger of religion and state in their time.
